blocks.text: Christ’s body stretches across the foreground, with His mother drawing close to His face. The picture includes several mourners against a blue field. The reproduction retains the fresco’s wall-painting character rather than presenting it as a portable wooden panel.

blocks.text: The catalogue identifies the Nerezi fresco near Skopje and dates the work to 1164. The historical artist is conventionally described as the Master of Nerezi. This is a particular medieval rendering of mourning and burial, with a visual arrangement beyond the wording of any one Gospel paragraph.

blocks.text:
And after this Joseph of Arimathaea, being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, besought Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus: and Pilate gave him leave. He came therefore, and took the body of Jesus.

And there came also Nicodemus, which at the first came to Jesus by night, and brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about an hundred pound weight.

Then took they the body of Jesus, and wound it in linen clothes with the spices, as the manner of the Jews is to bury.

Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden; and in the garden a new sepulchre, wherein was never man yet laid.

There laid they Jesus therefore because of the Jews’ preparation day; for the sepulchre was nigh at hand.
blocks.context: Canonical scriptural narrative in the identified historical English edition; later biographical traditions are separately attributed.
